utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the commander of the KLA says that nine KLA soldiers were killed in Racak, and he said that he had 47 soldiers. I am telling you that from their Staff we have operative information that there were about 80 members of the KLA in Racak and that the girl in question, who regrettably got killed in this clash with the police, got killed in the clash, was together with her brother and her father, a member of this terrorist group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't make myself clear. I'd like you, please, to give us the detail of why it is you say she's a member of the KLA. If the answer is you can't, say so and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've told you on the basis of which information I'm stating that. Operative information and intelligence indicated that, that she was a member of the KLA, too, and we've looked at that in the previous documents. Why would somebody say that someone was a member of a terrorist organisation if that person was not a member? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you direct us to the document in which it's recorded that she was a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot direct you this instant because there's about a hundred statements that indicate that, that only talk about this Racak group. We've already been through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll take Your Honour to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, how do you know she had a gun with her when she got killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see whether she had a rifle in her hands, but she certainly would not have got killed had she not had a rifle in her hands. Nobody would have shot at her if she didn't have a rifle in her hands. Had we found anything out along those lines, either I or the commanding officer in Racak, measures would have been taken against a person who would have shot at an unarmed person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let -- can we stay for a minute with one other paragraph - you've already looked at it - on Shukri Buja's statement. It's on the same page. Little bit further down, I think. Can you move the page down, please, Mr. Nort. Maybe the next page. There we are. That's fine. In this statement, as you've already explained, Shukri Buja identifies nine KLA soldiers killed in Racak, and indeed you can look elsewhere and there's a reference to others who were killed elsewhere at the same general time. You know, don't you, that dying for the KLA was a matter of honour for many people. Don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a matter for honour for who, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a matter of honour --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, a matter of honour? Well, I am telling you that at least 50 per cent of KLA members were forced into going out to fight. There is information to that effect. There is intelligence. Call other witnesses. Call other Albanians. Protect them. I'm telling you that they will tell them what happened -- tell you what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've seen books of the glorious fall of the KLA. We've heard accounts or we've discussed accounts of people wanting to be credited as dying for the KLA even when they had not done so, possibly because they could get a pension or financial benefits. There were many reasons why people would want to be described as dying, when they did die in battle, for the KLA. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly did die.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many certainly did die.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want your help with is this, if you possibly can, it's why I asked you the question I did at the beginning that Mr. Kay objected to: We see in his statement made in 2001 that Shukri Buja identified nine people of the KLA who died in battle on the 15th of January. He makes it clear that none of the other people who died in Racak, the 40-odd people who were found in Racak dead, were members of the KLA. I want you to help us, if you can, with whether there's any reason you can think of why those who died gloriously in battle, or even if not gloriously, in battle, should not be credited with their correct KLA status. Can you think of any reason?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you sure that this status had not been credited them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you think of a reason in the course of your answering questions to me, don't hesitate to interrupt me and we'll come back to that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, with the Court's leave, I want to ask this witness some questions about what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say something now in relation to this question, this question that you put to me just now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to view the funeral in Racak when Walker came to the mosque, when 40 coffins were lined up with the bodies of the persons who died in the terrorist -- anti-terrorist operation. All the coffins were covered with an Albanian flag, the Albanian flag, all of them. That happens only when a soldier is killed, a policeman, or a state official in the interests of the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made that point a couple of days ago or yesterday, and what you're suggesting is that there would have been some pride, if your account is right, there would be some pride in them dying for the cause. Can you think of any reason why these people and their bereaved relations would not claim them to have been KLA activists in death, especially if that role would bring them financial benefit in the form of pension? Can you think of any reason, Mr. Janicevic, why people would do that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean would they be proud after their death, after they had died? That's how I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there reason for these people who got killed not to be proud of the fact that they died for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. I've given him a chance to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, if Shukri Buja's statement was drafted after the indictment was public?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But of course it was taken on the usual terms, certainly. Your Honours, I wish to ask this witness some questions about what Goran Radosavljevic said in an interview, for his comments on those answers. We have a copy that can go on the overhead projector. The Court will remember that I've played to other witnesses what Goran Radosavljevic said to "The Death of Yugoslavia" interviewers, and I don't think there's any need to repeat that material. It will be in the Court's mind, having heard it twice. In light of the Court's practice, I am of course not seeking to put this material in as an exhibit, simply to have the witness's comment on the answers given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're getting it positioned on the screen, Mr. Janicevic, when did you last speak to Goran Radosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, is he still alive and well?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he's alive. I don't know whether he is well. That's a relative thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the video booth could focus, to assist our reading, on the bottom right-hand sector of this double page and enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of interview, and you'll see the format of this interview, Mr. Janicevic, we have both the English and the interpretation. So it's possible to see the whole interview as it's played out with sequential interpretation. He was asked: "The next topic is basically the Racak interview -- Racak issue." And asked: "If you could describe, give us an overview of what the planning for Racak and the conduct of the operation?" You will then see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, because there's a controversy as to the correctness of this interpretation, how about seeing the video ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is not a video -- it may be a video. This is an OTP interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it is a transcription of both the English and of the B/C/S spoken by the interviewee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happens is you have the interviewer asking the questions, you then have the -- as we're looking at it there on the screen, you have Mr. Coo asking, "If you could describe, give us an overview ..." You have the observation -- you have the interpreter putting that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- then you have the reply. And if we then turn over the page in the English, please, we have the answer: "Based on the information that would arrive as was the case with the paper that we just saw." Now, if we go down the page a little bit, what he says is this -- that's fine, thank you very much. He's asked the question: "Based on the fact that it was known --" Sorry, he makes the answer: "Based on the fact that it was known that a certain family from the village killed many members of the police." He then went on to say: "It was decided on a joint action of the police and the army against this village so we would attempt to reach the terrorists to get their equipment."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept what is recorded in this interview, that it was a joint operation, a joint action of the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept, and I don't see any reason for Goran Radosavljevic to say this. First of all, if it had been a joint operation of the army and police, the police would never have had to leave Racak at 1500 hours after a strong counter-attack by the terrorists, if the army had been helping them. Around 150 policemen were involved. Around 400 terrorists mounted a counter-attack, and that's why the police had to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he deals with the reason for the army's involvement a little later, but if the video booth and Mr. Nort would take us to the top right-hand part of this double sheet, he's asked: "Just before we go into it. Do you recall where the intelligence came from or the information that you based the operation on?" And his answer is: "The Secretariats in Urosevac." Do you agree with that answer?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no choice but to repeat myself a hundred times. I told you that my secretariat made a draft operations plan relying on prior intelligence and information about the activities of the terrorist organisation. The MUP staff approved this plan and the operation itself. A member of the Staff was appointed to lead this action. He was also appointed leader of the Operative Pursuit Group. There's nothing disputable about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't follow this interpretation. It seems that Radosavljevic spoke a bit longer than "The secretariats in Urosevac."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What you get is his answer, the interpreter says: "The secretariats in Urosevac"; he says, "Prizren"; the interpreter says, "Prizren"; from, he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The sentence which precedes "The secretariats in Urosevac" contains something related to Pristina and Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's correct, absolutely right, because what's happening is you're getting exactly what flows -- what comes from the tape, and so that he speaks in his own language, the interpreter starts the process of interpretation, he interrupts, "Prizren," and so the interpreter says "Prizren." He then says "State Security," he then says "and Military Intelligence Service." So that if and when it happens that the interviewee speaks over --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm addressing the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice is addressing the Court, so when he has finished, Mr. Milosevic, we'll hear from Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're getting exactly what's coming. There's no summarising, it's exactly what words come onto the tape. And in this particular example it would appear to be the case that the interpreter gives an answer, saying, "The secretariats in Urosevac," and Radosavljevic corrects that answer. And we can see why as well, because if you look at the answer given from "Iz Podrucnih..." et cetera, he makes no reference there in the first part to Urosevac. He makes reference to, apparently, Pristina and it's corrected to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon noticed the difference, the discrepancy between the lengths of answers in Serbian and in English, and I think it would be a logical solution to let the witness read the sentence so we can see what the matter is. The sentence is: "From local secretariats, that is secretariat of Pristina or, rather, not secretariat of Pristina but the secretariat in Urosevac." And the interpreter only says "The secretariat in Urosevac." That's what the sentence in Serbian says. And then the conversation goes on, but it's just a continuation, it's not a correction of what was said previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems to me the accused is right on that, that that's the answer that's given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page very briefly and then, more significantly, to the page after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next page, bottom right-hand corner, one detail here. That's fine. In the interview he says, through the interpreter: "They were told that there were no civilians in the village." Is it right that you were told - is this your position - that there were no civilians in the village or did you know there were civilians in the village? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that there was a total of about 50 civilians in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the next page, bottom left-hand sector to begin with, and we see PC, Mr. Coo, saying: "The next steps, you had the meeting, you developed this plan. What would the next step be to transform this plan into an order?" The question is interpreted. Mr. Radosavljevic gives an answer which is to this effect: "After the meeting all the participants that were in charge of their units signed the plan." He then said: "Since the VJ and the MUP participated, one plan went to the Joint Command." So he uses the word "Joint Command." He goes on to say: "And as far as I know, this plan was approved." Do you agree with the two parts of that answer given by Mr. Radosavljevic, first that both parts signed the plan; and second, that the plan went to the Joint Command for approval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the Chamber give me leave to explain where this plan was made and where it was approved and who approved it in order not to be engulfed in these lies, because Goran Radosavljevic is lying, and I'll explain even why he's lying. May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was on the 12th of January. Prior to that, operative intelligence was sent to the MUP staff in Pristina about the events taking place in Stimlje municipality on the axis towards Dulje, in the Crnoljevo gorge, and on the Pristina-Urosevac road. On the 12th, at my briefing with my commanders, I agreed that we would make a draft plan for an anti-terrorist action to be submitted to the Staff in Urosevac because we knew by that time that there was a large terrorist group of about 80 men headed by Afet Bilalli, nicknamed Qopa, who were mounting daily attacks on the road, targeting anything that moves. They were kidnapping innocent people, stopping traffic, attacking police and army convoys. The last in the series of attacks was the attack on Slivovo village where policeman Przic was killed. I sent this plan to Pristina, to the MUP staff. I asked leave from the Chamber to explain how the plan was made, and the president of the Chamber allowed me to do so. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Come to the point, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived at the Staff, I presented this plan in the presence of Staff Commander Lukic and head of department Vlastimir Djordjevic. I told them about everything that was going on. They had known some of this information from before. They looked at the plan, and they accepted it. Goran Radosavljevic, as Staff member, was appointed to lead this action. The action was agreed to take police on the 13th. However, on the 13th, it was not carried out because the weather did not allow it. It was too cold and there were other problems as well. We postponed it until the 15th. On the 14th, in the evening, at the office of the head of SUP, that's where I was, in addition to company commanders, the chief of the police station was invited, Goran Radosavljevic as well, as well as the leader of the Operative Pursuit Group and platoon commanders, and Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear which colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who was only invited to acquaint himself with the plan. There was no signing. Nobody signed. Radosavljevic, the Colonel Krsman Jelic, or anybody else. The plan was only approved, and the approval process is done on the map, including the participation of the head of department, because all the pre-conditions had been created for mounting this anti-terrorist operation and for eliminating this terrorist group that had already wielded a lot of evil in this area. Goran Radosavljevic appointed his deputy, late Mr. Mekic, to lead this group, and he appeared in this area at 3.30. He hadn't been there before. He had radio communication with his subordinates before, but he only showed up on the spot at 3.30. The Operative Pursuit Group was on the positions that they had occupied in the morning, and they were told to go down, although it had been previously agreed for them to hold those positions until the on-site investigation team arrived. As soon as they did, the terrorist attack on a huge scale started. I had never seen anything like it before. They were shooting from all sides, and the policemen on the on-site investigation team had to pull out quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rather move away from the issues that we were dealing with and I'll come back to your description of the attack shortly, but Radosavljevic was your superior, wasn't he? Goran Radosavljevic was your superior?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not exactly my superior, but he was the superior of that anti-terrorist group that mounted the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give any explanation for how he, out of his own mouth, refers to a body in place in January 1999 known as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Radosavljevic was a major on the police force at the time, and he was leader of the Operative Pursuit Group. I don't know the answer to your question. You would have to ask him. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, please, Mr. Nort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, did you say that Colonel Krsman Jelic was the only person that participated at the meeting on the 14th from VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The only representative of the army of Yugoslavia as commander of the 243rd Motorised Brigade who attended this meeting only for information purposes, to acquaint himself with the plan of the operation to avoid friendly fire during the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Nobody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody else. I claim that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, left-hand side, middle of the page. Mr. Coo asked Radosavljevic: "You recall -- I know that you don't know the VJ unit name -" something he dealt with earlier - "but the type of units, were the VJ providing infantry or artillery or tanks or all of the above?" And he said, "I think it was a tank unit. They had other armoured vehicles within it also." Right about that, was he?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an artillery tank unit that was part of the border battalion, as far as I know and as far as I understand things military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go on one, two -- can we go on four pages, please, Mr. Nort. One, two, three, four. And if I can just look at the top to make sure we're at the right place. Yes. Halfway down that page, on the left-hand side, Mr. Coo asked Radosavljevic: "Why was it necessary --" further down. That's fine. "Why was it necessary to have VJ infantry as well? Was there not sufficient MUP personnel to do this?" Answer: "Yes. The police didn't have enough men." Is that the truth of why this joint plan went to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. The police had 130 men involved in that anti-terrorist operation, and according to plan, there was not a single one more. That was enough to perform this assignment and to eliminate the activity of this terrorist group, because we opted for a different system of blockade and encirclement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then finally, on the bottom right-hand side of this sheet, please, I think you'll agree with this material: " ... General Djordjevic was close to the scene, was he in a police station or a command post?" And Radosavljevic said: "I later heard he was in the police station, and I met him at night in the evening." Next page, top left-hand corner, please, Mr. Nort. "Which police station was that?" "The police station in Stimlje, which was the closest police station." Then a couple of questions further down: "General Lukic, was he in the immediate area of the operation ..." Answer: "I think he was in the Staff, because I talked to him through the radio a few times." Do you agree with all that about Djordjevic and Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lukic was at the Staff and Djordjevic was at the Staff too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the police station --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- may I just explain, please. At 11.00, Djordjevic came to the police station in Stimlje with his driver. He came to make inquiries, to find out how the operation was coming along, and at 11.30 he left for Pristina. Therefore, Goran Radosavljevic had not the slightest chance to meet him at the police station in Stimlje. General Djordjevic spent 30 minutes at the police station all in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about contacts with --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't even sit down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... did you make phone calls to Mr. Sainovic or did --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What contact?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there phone calls made to Sainovic from your police station?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never spoken to Sainovic in my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of his speaking to anybody else at your police station?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody from the police station, no. No, not from the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The position is that there had to be a joint operation and a Joint Command because of the believed, and indeed accurately believed, presence of KLA in villages other than at Racak. They had to be pinned down, didn't they, if you were to get into Racak, to stop them coming to the Defence of those in Racak?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at your own Defence tab 13, you had 60 in Rance, 200 in Petrovo, 40 in Malopoljce, a hundred in Racak, and 50 in Luzak, you couldn't go into Racak without defending yourselves against what the KLA from those neighbouring locations might do, could you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you don't know the configuration of the terrain, you keep Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. saying such things. I'm telling you that we could do that. The police was there -- the police who were there from 6.30 onwards were able to protect the on-site investigation team and prevent anyone else from entering the village. However, due to a mistake in command, it so happened that the terrorists were able to reoccupy the positions that they had been driven away from before 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, if you looked at, or if we look at Shukri Buja's statement, he makes it quite clear that in the middle of the day they were defeated, but by the end of the day they'd retaken positions. Do you agree with that observation of him? You can find that in the English version at about page 14 in a paragraph beginning: "At 11.30 hours I gave the order to regain the positions." And you'll find that, I think, at the foot of page 13.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he describes defeat, retreat, and retaking of positions. He's right about that, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Retaking of positions. It was due to the error made by the commander leading the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a matter of fact, in Shukri Buja's analysis of what happened on the 15th, where he says that the KLA were caught by surprise, a number got killed, they withdrew, they then retook positions at 11.30, he's accurate in his description of what happened.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His description is correct, but look at the paragraph before that. The soldiers were coming into Luzak one after the other, and the stories were so confusing that some said that only three to four survived and the rest were killed. If several or maybe dozens fled from the front line and the rest were killed, what would that have meant?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shall we go on to the next paragraph but two and then I think I'm finished with Mr. Buja's statement probably. There may be a couple of points, but if we look on a couple of paragraphs we see -- it will be either further down the page, Mr. Nort, or the next page. Next page, please. And for you, Mr. Janicevic, it will be on page 14, I think, where at the top or in the middle it says these two things: First it says, "The deputy commander reported that the second plan of action was achieved that the Luzak border was controlled. We concluded that the Serb Forces were not going to fight through the night, and we decided to attack at 1600 hours to regain the positions and to find our missing soldiers. It was not the first time that the Serbs did this. It was characteristic of them not to fight throughout the night. They usually just shelled areas after dark." Is he right about that? Is that the way the VJ operated?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. I have explained how it came about that the police left Racak and that the terrorists were able to retake their positions from which they had mounted that attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, one thing is clear, that following their retreat and temporary defeat, they retook possession of the territory, and they remained in possession, because when we see the video the following day of Ambassador Walker and General Drewienkiewicz and others observing the bodies, we know that there were KLA soldiers present. So they regained the territory, and they kept it, didn't they, for the 16th?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want now to go to some of the documents in the collection of Racak documents. I don't know if the Chamber has brought those with them, but we'll lay them on the overhead projector if not. And I want in a minute to go back to that document we were looking at yesterday, but I want to explore your knowledge, please, Mr. Janicevic, on the 15th. You were at the police station. I accept it's only a couple hundred metres away from the beginnings of Racak, although there's a hill, I think, there. What was your source of information in the course of that day as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information that I received through radio communication from the participants in the action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And when did you return to Urosevac police station, what time?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime around 1900 hours. I can't remember exactly, but towards evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that after the return of the various forces from the area, the police forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police forces stayed in the area. Just one platoon returned, and that one was attacked, by the village of Kosare, I think it was, while they were returning to the police station, from a hand-held rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to look at this document, which I think we looked at yesterday. This is tab 5 of the Racak documents, but it is, as an exhibit, 156, tab 16; alternatively 320, tab 27. Now, Mr. Janicevic, this is a document of yours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sent at 1932 hours in the evening.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you produce this document to us as one of your documents? Because you didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please repeat the answer, Mr. Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I didn't have it. I wasn't in possession of it, Your Honour, this document, and so I -- and I couldn't find it in the archives of the Urosevac SUP either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You looked for it, did you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask for this document specifically. I asked for all the documents that would be relevant to these proceedings, but this document wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This one simply wasn't there, was it? It's a document of the kind that had to be retained, didn't it? Because it was indeed produced, I think, to the Prosecution in various ways.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was just a mistake, then, in your records; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. Had we stayed at the positions we were until 1999, all the documents would be here. All the documents would be in their proper place. But unfortunately, we weren't able to stay on there and so most of the documents were lost without any trace. And what you managed to find in the ministry, the headquarters of the ministry, or the centre, communications centre, that's it, and perhaps some other document which the members of the police had taken with their personal archives and the cases that they were involved in and that they were issued and needed to return.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be given a copy of that document to have a look at it, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was given yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I can't keep producing it every day, the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was produced long ago in the Racak binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was produced in the Racak binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think I have a spare hard copy for him today. He'll have to watch it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Kwon will make his available to you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I did invite the parties, including the accused, to bring their Racak papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, this was sent to Belgrade, wasn't it. Crime investigation administration, police administration, operations centre Belgrade. This would be a document kept in multiple copies, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there ought to be multiple copies. Under normal conditions, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at what's said on it as a document coming from you -- let's see what is said. On the first page, reference to 0300 hours. The next paragraph, that the battle with terrorists lasting until 1530 hours. The terrorist group was liquidated with maximum effort. Reference to the encircling operation and an injured policeman, Trajkovic. Then the reference to the horseshoe ambush that we covered yesterday. We'll just look at the second half of that, so I'll read the paragraph: "The horseshoe ambush was applied in the blockade and it was laid between the villages of Luznica and Rance, behind terrorist trenches and connecting trenches. During action by the unit and attempts to arrest members of the terrorist gang, police fell into the ambush. They opened fire at the same time and after some hours of fighting they were liquidated. Even though they'd been called on to surrender, none of the terrorists wanted to do so." Can you just explain the meaning of that paragraph and the basis of your information on which it was based.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the dispatch explains it. There's just an error in the fact that it's not Luznica but Luzak and Rance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So that takes us to a slightly different part of -- or a significantly different part of the territory, but what you're describing is -- we can't see it on this map, we can only see it on the bigger map -- efforts to arrest the terrorist gang, but even though called on, they didn't want to surrender. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that they took up arms and opened fire at the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the trenches and from the houses and from the yards, from the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that? Where's the reference, please, to houses, yards, and streets in this report of yours made the same day on the basis of information coming to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a preliminary report. You see it says here that about 60 members were liquidated. It's still not a report after an on-site investigation having been conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we going to find a report of yours that says something about the locations of the places where people died, or will it always read as though they died in the trenches, Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean "always read that they died in the trenches"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever set out an account based on information suggesting that these people who were found had died in streets and in yards and in houses? Did you ever?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a man of letters, an author to write stories. I wrote reports on the basis -- or, rather, to my superior command about what I received from the people who took part in the action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So let's go to the next paragraph of this document that you didn't bring with you, which starts off with: "About 60 members of the Albanian terrorist gangs were liquidated." Well, 60 is a bit much because -- no, it's not, actually, if you add the KLA nine plus the 40-odd of the people who were found, it's getting up towards 60. How did you get the figure of 60 on the very day, the 15th of January, when you hadn't seen the bodies yourself, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the report that my subordinates provided. On the basis of assumptions of the anti-terrorist actions that had been completed. And if you read what it says at the end here, you'll see. These are not the exact data, not the right facts, that an investigation would take place and that after an on-site investigation has taken place the number of killed members of terrorist bands would be ascertained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, it is quite close, isn't it? It's quite close, 60 to about 50, the mid-50s, of people who died in Racak in the course of that day's operation. Tell us, did individual soldiers from whom we haven't heard report, "I think killed two people here"? "I think I killed one person there"? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, how were you able to put "about 60"?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leaders of the organisations of units who worked there, the platoon commanders and the company commander, they wrote a report, and on the basis of their assessments, they estimated that about 60 Siptar terrorists were killed in that operation. That is their assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have these reports before you by 1932 hours when you dictated or typed this document?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They conveyed it to me orally, and after that, the next day, I received a written report as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So somewhere, although it may not have been found, there's a written report setting out about in total -- or giving an account that totals about 60 dead people; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those reports it says that these people were killed in combat and in the fighting with members of the police, and I'm sure there are reports of that kind in the ministry. When they gave you this, they should have given you that, too, which would be the foundations for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can be sure, Mr. Janicevic, that we have asked every person we can for documents, and we have found no document thus far that gives an account of people dying and where they died. Shall we read on, because this is your document contemporaneous. You deal with Marinkovic, and then you say this: "No civilians were hurt during the execution of the operation." How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the report, Mr. Nice. I asked whether there were any civilians who had been killed or injured, and they told me there were no casualties, and that was contained in the written report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then saw three Brownings, two carbines, and 36 automatic rifles were found. That's the only reference to the weapons that were found at that stage, yes?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the stage when the anti-terrorist operation had been completed, is that what you mean? At the end of the operation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the only place in this particular dispatch, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the truth is that those weapons, those 36 automatic rifles, were either found in their base or they were found in trenches, but they weren't found anywhere else, were they? That's where they were found, those 36 weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the reports which I received, all the weapons were found -- or, rather, only one rifle which was handmade was found in the command at headquarters. Everything else was found on the spot around the people who had lost their lives in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... people who had lost their lives. Well, tell us a bit more about that, because this is, you see, the very first time that this Court has ever heard about this. So you tell us about it. You tell us what your source of information is, and where it's recorded, and so on.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of my information, and I'm repeating this for the hundredth time, were the reports from the leaders or commanders of the platoons and companies and the pursuit group at that time. Those people who were in the field, on the ground, they are the ones who submitted reports and told me what had happened on site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And an exact count of 1.802 rounds had already been made, had it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pieces of ammunition, pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's move on --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... -- may, to tab 6, please, in the same document. This is a document that's only available in English. It's report from one of the OSCE monitors. It starts off on the 15th of January, saying that they heard of the engagement west of Stimlje, that this group arrived when most of the firing had stopped, at 1730 hours, that they assisted in the movement of casualties, four adults and one child. They had a direct given for a meeting the following morning. Then on the following morning, on the 16th of January when there had been a briefing, they went off and had a meeting with the MUP chief in Urosevac. That would be you, would it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage, the OSCE, and we can see this from the foot of this page, were aware of numbers of people being killed, apparently at close range, and at that stage it was thought a group of ten who appeared to have been mowed down. There was also a 12-year-old boy and some other males. So that was the state of knowledge of the OSCE when they came to meet you. And the next thing that I want you to look at, please, is tab 7A, which is your own document. This is at tab 64.8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is tab 6 an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, tab 6 is an exhibit. 180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it refers to a report of the meeting with the MUP chief in Urosevac being attached. Is that the document, the second page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I don't think it is, and I think we'll have to find that a little later for you. It comes about tab 9, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I want, first of all, to look at this document, which you have produced yourself as tab 64.8, and this is dated the 16th of January of 1999. We can see that, if we look at the last paragraph, it must be a late document because it purports to cover the whole period of that day, although at the first paragraph -- no, maybe it covers the period until 1700 hours. When did you write this document?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly when I wrote the document. I wrote documents of this kind all the time. Probably after the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which case then it may help the Chamber if we instead move to tab 9 first. No, in fact I'm going to change that so the Chamber has things in order. If we go to tab 8 first. This is not a document you can help us with very much, but I'll just draw it to everyone's attention. This is -- picks up the accounting process when the OSCE went and spoke to Petrovic, the liaison officer for the VJ. Now, you weren't there at this meeting, which was at 10.37 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petrovic, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to give a sequence to events. The OSCE went to Petrovic. This was Maisonneuve and others. That's the right -- we can see Maisonneuve at the top and Petrovic and Gilbertson and others, the interpreter. And then did you know this: That they raised with Petrovic -- in the middle of the page but further down, Mr. Nort, please. Maisonneuve suggested to Petrovic: "Who coordinated tank fire on the civilian houses when no persons were firing back, when there was smoke from chimneys, with families in basements?" He said, "Professional armies don't do these things but we may expect it from the MUP." He went on to say that: "The execution of 50 people is of War Crimes Tribunal stuff." Petrovic had nothing to say to that and indeed went on to say what they were doing was normal tasks and exercises. Now, did you know -- did Petrovic get in touch with you, as his opposite number, to tell him what the OSCE were inquiring into?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the name of Petrovic, I hear that name for the first time. I knew quite a number of army officers, but this man Petrovic, perhaps if I were to see him I might recognise him, but just going by the name, no man by the name of Petrovic contacted me at all or asked me about the -- my contacts with the verifiers, with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see as well on this page he also, however, said that Stimlje was done by the MUP with a Praga, AVs, and one tank. Can you explain how your military counterpart, as he was, liaison officer counterpart in any event, would be suggesting that the -- a tank and Pragas were involved in the overall Stimlje attack?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no attack on Stimlje. I beg to differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that exhibit, Your Honours, was -- or is 177. If we can go to tab 9, which is Exhibit 179, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12:44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 9 of the Jasovic -- of the Racak papers is Exhibit number 179. It's on the overhead projector. It's in English. And it records the second meeting that they had with the OSCE - Maisonneuve, Gilbertson, and others - with you, at 11.14 on the morning of the 16th, asking what happened in Racak. You maintained that you were in charge of four communities, including Stimlje, and you spoke of terrorist attacks, the police blocking the roads to Racak, and of meeting strong resistance to entrance at Racak. Do you remember saying those things? Not remember, do you accept that you would have said those things?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember saying, that there was an attack at the entrance to Racak? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept that you would have told the OSCE that police blocked the roads to Racak but met strong resistance at the entrance to Racak?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the OSCE that the police this blocked Racak from the Stimlje access, not only the road, and that it came upon strong resistance on the 15th at the very entrance to Racak at 0700 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then you went on to explain about the terrorists who had been killed. Do you remember the last document we looked at? You gave a global figure of 60, which is roughly right for the total number of people killed. You may not read English, but you can see what's been recorded by the OSCE. You said 15 terrorists were killed. Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the clash with the police, at least 15 terrorists were killed, because those are the figures that -- that was the figure that we had. That was the established figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean established --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to misinform, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you do you mean "established"? Because you'd sent a telegram the previous day, and you told us about your sources of information, where you said about 60 members of the Albanian terrorist groups were liquidated and no civilians were injured. Why have you suddenly reduced the total number of people killed to approximately the correct number of terrorists, as you would describe the KLA? Why have you reduced it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first official information that went to the Staff and was published by the Staff was that at least 15 terrorists had been killed. Until an on-site investigation is carried out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you find that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the dispatches of the Urosevac SUP sent out to the Staff. Where you found the other dispatch that you read from a moment ago, that's where you'll find the other one as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. The one -- we're dealing with things in date order. Do you remember I said to you yesterday it's important isn't it, you know this as a policeman, to look at documents contemporaneous to events. On the 15th of January, you sent a message, a carefully crafted message, to Belgrade, saying 60 members of Albanian terrorist gangs were liquidated. No ifs or buts about it. Now, when the community, the international community appears, you spoke only of about 15, which is about right, because as well as the ones who died in Racak, there were others who were killed in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. location. We can find reference to that. Why are you suddenly changing your position, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not changing my position. What I told you was this, and I state again, that the first piece of information that went to the Ministry of the Interior and the MUP staff was -- referred to at least 15 terrorists. Now, until the end of the investigation, nobody --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- had the right -- please may I be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may, but I want you to --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't show you that, but you have all the mechanisms to access that material. So when you received the dispatch, you could have received the other one. It's a short one, just five or six lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you could have taken that as well, and it was dated the 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this something you've remembered all morning while I've been asking you methodically, almost slowly times, to go through the history, is it something you've always remembered that you sent a first record of 15 going? Is that right? And that somehow that record's been mislaid or lost or gone up in flames?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, at the moment you asked me about Vlastimir Djordjevic, whether he came or not, I said then, too, that Vlastimir Djordjevic received information in the police station of Stimlje whereby, according to knowledge gained so far, at least 15 terrorists had been killed, according to what we knew up until that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice is giving the witness the impression that he's quoting from the document, and the witness cannot read English. And he said a few moments ago that it was 15, whereas what it says in the text is, "Suspect 15 terrorists killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we note that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the witness doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he knows now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think he still knows, because it hasn't been interpreted for him. I am on the Serbian channel, but I haven't heard the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, would you just read that portion so that it may be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, the OSCE monitors, seeing you at 1114 hours on the 16th of January, 1999, recorded your explanation as the following, and I quote: "Suspect 15 terrorists killed." And to set it in context, you're recorded then as saying: "Tried to find them, no one in village, went to forest and bunkers little bit up from village." Now, back to where we were. Tell us, please, what was the document --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Could you repeat this last bit? Who was it that went to the forest and who was it that they couldn't find?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are your words recorded by OSCE in obviously abbreviated form. I will repeat them. "Suspect 15 terrorists killed. Tried to find them, no one in village, went to forest and bunkers little bit up from village." That's what you're recorded as saying.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is sheer confusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. This is not what I talked about when I talked to the representatives of the OSCE. I told you what I told them. If they shortened things in order to save paper or time or whatever, I told you what I said to them. I said that at least 15 terrorists were killed in the fighting. That is an official figure until the on-site investigation was carried out, and that is what I pointed out to them. Until the on-site investigation was carried out, we could not give the exact information as to how many casualties there were. Mr. Gilbertson at one point got up and said, "Sir, we're already carrying out an on-site investigation." And I said, "Mr. Gilbertson, in what capacity are you carrying out an on-site investigation? Are you an investigating judge, are you a policeman, are you the district public prosecutor? In what capacity are you carrying out an on-site investigation? And he said to me, please, it's been 27 years now that I've been a policeman and I know how this is done. I'm not challenging that, but in my country, and it's still my country, on-site investigations should be carried out in accordance with the laws of my country. That's what I said to them and I have no reason to lie. I have no reason to lie or not to say the truth, to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One possibility might be that the observers revealed that they now knew the truth, and you knew you were caught. It might be that they revealed to you what they'd seen or what they'd heard about the total number of people killed, and you knew at that stage you were only ever going to be able to identify about 15 who were terrorists. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true that that's what I thought. You don't know what I was thinking, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me. You seem to have a good recollection of what Mr. Gilbertson said.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I thought what I said. I said that at least 15 terrorists, to the best of our knowledge, got killed in the clash with the police. Further on, I said that they would get official information at the moment when the on-site investigation finishes, because that was the plan, that on that day the on-site investigation team should go out to the actual site. And he answered to me that they were already carrying out an on-site investigation. Since they were carrying out the on-site investigation, they know best what was going on. But again, I claim, had there been any intention -- let me just finish. Please let me finish. Had there been any intention along the lines of what you've been saying about what you're trying to prove, do you think we would have informed the verifiers to be there at 7.00 in the morning to observe the entire course of the anti-terrorist operation? Would we have informed the media?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're moving off the topic.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How was the conversation between the verifier and yourself recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The verifiers were probably taking notes of their own. I kept notes of my own. I reported to my superiors and they probably reported to their superiors, through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you see them taking notes at the time when you spoke, so that when you said at least 15 were killed, did you see them write that down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see that. I didn't see whether they wrote it down or not, but I assume they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that's what you said, at least 15 were killed, and they apparently wrote down, "Suspect 15 killed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see whether they wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, as head of the secretariat, did not have the right to provide information without an investigating judge, because the investigation had already started. The investigation had already started, and the investigating judge is the only person who can provide information to the public and to the Verification Mission as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that day that person was in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we appear to be fighting shadows again because there doesn't seem to be a dispute that at this stage the figure was 15. What's concerning me more is if we went back to tab 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- if you're looking at tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and the bottom paragraph on the first page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- where there's a link made between 60 and the presence of the investigative judge. I don't know if you want to explore that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may do. In fact, in my sequence of questions it wasn't one I thought of but I may come back to it, and I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can understand the point of questioning here. So it is your point that when he said, "Suspect 15 terrorists had been killed," this is true?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is that he lied to the Belgrade when he reported in a dispatch when he said 60 terrorists were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 60 is the total number of people killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Total.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 45 plus 9 is about 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he says here Albanian terrorists. I see the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And if the Court will allow me, there's a sequence of questions and you're going to see how things develop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court will allow me, we'll see how things develop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can deal with one matter, because page 2 of this document the witness is asked to confirm a precise figure right in the middle - I don't want to be accused of leading or anything like that - and the Trial Chamber will see the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only too happy to take the witness to it, and indeed I probably will in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I hope so, because it says, "Can't say precisely."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 2 of tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Page 2 of the document. I'm doing it off the original exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can go back to where I was. Mr. Janicevic, I want you to -- not to divert from the question. Focus on it, and then we'll move on. You must understand that there is an inconsistency between writing on the 15th of January in the document to which His Honour Judge Bonomy has just drawn your attention that 60 members of an Albanian terrorist gang were liquidated, and indeed that the investigative judge came onto the scene but couldn't investigate matters further, and your then writing -- not writing, your then being recorded the following day as saying "Suspect 15 terrorists killed," or as Mr. Kay helpfully reminds us, can't say precisely it was 15 but something about that. Now, can you explain, for example - and I'll give you a few possibilities - why didn't -- could -- is there a document that you sent to someone that says, "Well, we've heard it's 60 but we only know about 15"?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I don't know whether the interpreters are not capable of translating what I've been saying. I am speaking very clearly in my mother tongue. I said that in the clash with the police, according to our knowledge, at least 15 terrorists were killed. I did not say that that is what was suspected, that they were killed or wounded, but that that is what is believed. That is the information we had when we had these talks on the 15th of January. On the 15th of January, the on-site investigation started at 1530 hours. Danica Marinkovic, investigating judge, and the deputy district public prosecutor were at the investigation. At that moment, the Secretariat of the Interior no longer -- is no longer in charge. We stop giving any information about the site itself and what is going on there. The dispatch that was sent to the MUP is by way of information, and it can be corrected during the course of the investigation or the end of the investigation. Well, what I can tell you is that even now we don't know how many got killed there. Although Mr. Nice is trying to prove that there was 45, I'm saying even now that I don't know how many. First of all, we did not carry out the on-site investigation. Officially we never fully completed the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me how the figure changed from 60 to 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no change. The dispatch that was sent to the Ministry of the Interior at 1900 hours on Friday the 15th is on the basis of free estimates of members of the police who were engaged in the anti-terrorist operation. These are their reports. That was their assumption. One platoon said, for example, ten. Another one said 20. Another one said 30. So the figure adds up to about 50 or 60. That's just an assumption. That is an assumption that was not confirmed and that can either be confirmed or refuted ultimately at the end of the on-site investigation, because the investigation is the one that resolves the entire problem. However, we could not complete it on the 15th or on the 16th or on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how did it -- by 11.00 the following morning, how had it changed to 15 - simple question - without the investigation having proceeded any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, the answer is very simple too. The answer is simple too. On the 15th of January, the official information that was bandied about was at least 15 terrorists. That is the official information. What was sent to the ministry was unconfirmed, unofficial, and that can only be confirmed by the end of the investigation, whether it was 40, 45, 49, or 60. Really, I still do not know the actual number of fatalities because we have not completed the investigation. Not because we didn't want to but because we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why -- I mean, others may be satisfied with this. I'm bamboozled by it. How do you manage to write to your official body, one step up from you, the Staff, and tell them 60? Why do that when the best you can actually say is there's at least 15? I mean, there's a huge discrepancy between these figures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the dispatch of -- containing the words "about 15" went to the MUP about 1400 hours, stating that at least 15 terrorists were killed in the fighting with the police. This dispatch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't seen that document, have I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, we haven't seen it. It's not available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it went from at least 15, up to 60, and then back down to at least 15; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me put the position to you and then --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, the translation was wrong and that's why the witness reacted, that that was not mentioned. Because Mr. Bonomy said, as far as I can see in the transcript, 15 and then 60, and then down to at least 15, and the Serbian interpretation said 50, 5-0. So the Serbian interpretation was wrong. Instead of saying 15, as Mr. Bonomy said, the Serbian interpretation was 50. That is why the witness is reacting, that that figure was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what happened, Mr. Janicevic, was this: When the OSCE came in on this morning, you realised that you'd been caught because they suggested to you a high number, and you knew, and you gave the game away that you could only ever prove that 15 of the people who died were terrorists, and without being able to set a better plan, you just told the truth. That's what happened, isn't it? They suspected a high number, and you knew you could never prove that high number were terrorists.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the OSCE come in and suggest a higher number?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're sure about that, are you? Are you sure about that? Are you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, please repeat what you just said. The interpreters didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The OSCE suggested that the number was larger than the number they heard from me, that's correct. But what I said to them was that we have unverified information, but until the investigation is completed, we will not be able to give them anything officially because we don't know the actual number of fatalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's go and have a look at the document that will help us a little bit on this. It's one of your own documents, and I think you've just remembered what you wrote. It's tab 64.8. And you can have the original. We'll have to come back to the tab we're looking at, otherwise we'll get bogged down forever, but I do need to go back to it. Let's just look at what you actually said yourself by way of a record of this meeting. On the 16th of January, the day after your previous document, you wrote to Belgrade -- well, the MUP staff in Pristina you wrote, and towards the bottom of the page - bit further down, please. B/C/S coming your way, I hope. Thank you very much. "On the 16th of January, 1999 --" perhaps you could make sure the witness has the B/C/S version. He will want to check the figures. From 11.00 to 12.00 a meeting was held with Dilbedson, Maisonneuve, and the chief of the Urosevac SUP. It goes on: "They asked questions concerning the police operation in Racak, which had been carried out in order to catch a terrorist group which had been stationed in that village and for which there had been information and intelligence to the effect that it had carried out eight terrorist acts in the Urosevac SUP ..." And it goes on a bit. Go over to the next paragraph. "When Vel --" that's Vel Dilbedson -- "asked what kind of police operation it was, he was told it was a classic police operation, which had been held in order to catch a terrorist group and put an end to its further activity in the area. He was told that Racak village had been blocked from the direction of Stimlje and the Stimlje-Racak road ..." It goes on a bit, further down that paragraph, and if I miss anything anybody wants me to read, they'll shout. "Having searched the village, despite fierce resistance from the terrorists, who dug in, the police took control of their positions and liquidated a number of terrorists, while some terrorists withdrew in the direction of Krsine hill. Several policemen neutralised the fire from the Browning and the machine-gun was taken to the centre of Racak to an on-site investigation ..." Next paragraph: "They were also told --" So you're simply, in this document, you're setting out what you said to the OSCE, not necessarily what was true. You said: "They were told that the police had not chased any terrorists beyond the trenches and connecting trenches, towards the woods, except for a group of policemen who had been sent to neutralise the Browning and who had carried out the assignment and returned to the centre of the village." Next paragraph: "Vel was interested solely in 'who planned the police operation, what weapons ... police members from other areas ...'" and so on. Next paragraph: "When he said that more than 50 civilians had been killed in the Racak village area, he was told that, according to our information, at least 15 terrorists had been killed and no civilians at all, and that the policemen had not been able to continue searching the terrain for security reasons and so we did not know whether more terrorists had been killed." Now, then, would you like to explain to us how 15 went down -- sorry. How 60 went down to 15, even qualified in the way you've got it here? How did you identify the 15 as terrorists?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat this to you once again, but please listen so that you'd be able to understand. On the 15th of January, a dispatch was sent to the Ministry of the Interior and to the Staff, informing them around 1400 hours that the operation was still underway and that, according to preliminary information, in the fighting at least 15 terrorists were killed. The investigation started at 1530 hours. The investigation team went to the site. At that moment, no one, according to the law, had the right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to interrupt at that point because that's the very point that Mr. Milosevic corrected the translation of from 15 to 50 a short while ago, and now the witness is again, according to the interpretation I'm getting, saying 15 at 1400 on the 15th. So we're become -- it is in fact from 15 up to 60 and back down to 15. Please carry on. The point would have passed if it hadn't been made just now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are talking about two different days, the 15th and the 16th of January. On the 15th of January, one dispatch was sent to the Ministry in which it was stated that in that area, in fighting with the police, at least 15 terrorists were killed. On the 16th, a group of verifiers came to the SUP with a view to receiving information as to what was going on there or what had happened there, although they knew better than we did what was going on on the ground. They asked me, and I told them what I knew and what I had to tell them. I had to tell them, because the investigation had already started.
